comm.t: Medhas goes on telling King Suratha (with the merchant Samādhi listening) the second story. Chapter 2 ended with the Goddess, her lion and her gaṇas destroying Mahiṣa’s army (2.67–69); chapter 3 brings out his generals one by one and then Mahiṣa himself. In recitation this mantra carries the bīja ॐ, which belongs to the pāṭha, not to the verse.

sandhi.note: The t of तत् stays unvoiced before s; the final m of सैन्यम् is simply pronounced with the following vowel (सैन्यमवलोक्य). The words are only written together.
Visarga before c becomes s, and s next to c becomes ś.
Final t becomes d before the voiced y.
a + a → ā (अथ + अम्बिकाम् → अथाम्बिकाम्). Inside the compound महासुरः the same rule joins महा + असुर.

samasa.sense: a mighty demon — the standard epithet of Mahiṣa’s captains

samasa.type: upapada tatpuruṣa (with the root-noun नी, affix kvip)

morph.note: Passive present participle: the passive stem हन्य- (√हन् + yak) with -मान. ‘Being slain’ — the slaughter of 2.67–69 is still going on as Cikṣura looks.
Perfect of √या: roots in -ā take the ending -औ in the 3rd singular (य-यौ).
Infinitive of √युध्: dh + t becomes ddh (युध् + तुम् → योद्धुम्), with guṇa of the root vowel. It expresses purpose after a verb of motion: ‘went to fight’.

mantras.anvaya: अथ महासुरः सेनानीः चिक्षुरः तत् सैन्यं निहन्यमानम् अवलोक्य कोपात् अम्बिकां योद्धुं ययौ।
mantras.anvaya_en: Subject with two appositions (महासुरः सेनानीः चिक्षुरः); an absolutive clause (सैन्यं निहन्यमानम् अवलोक्य); the main verb ययौ with a purpose infinitive.
mantras.lit: Having seen that army being slaughtered, the great asura, the general Cikṣura, in anger then went to fight Ambikā.
mantras.tr: Seeing his army cut down, the mighty asura Cikṣura, Mahiṣa’s general, went in fury to fight Ambikā.
mantras.tr_note: ‘His army’ and ‘Mahiṣa’s general’ make explicit what तत् and सेनानीः imply (Cikṣura is named Mahiṣa’s general at 2.40).

comm.t: The general steps forward when the army falls. Cikṣura was named first among Mahiṣa’s commanders at 2.40; now he faces the Goddess alone.

In the Gita Press pāṭha, chapters 2–4 form the middle carita, whose presiding form is Mahālakṣmī (a liturgical attribution). Chapter 3 is its battle: the generals fall one by one (3.2–20) before Mahiṣa himself comes forward (3.21).

sandhi.note: The visarga of सः is dropped before a consonant. The m of देवीम् becomes anusvāra before ś (मोऽनुस्वारः, 8.3.23).
-e + a- → -e’-: the initial a is absorbed; the avagraha marks it.
Before ś the visarga may stay (as printed here) or become ś (मेरुगिरेश्शृङ्गम्); the Gita Press keeps it.

samasa.vigraha: मेरुः च असौ गिरिः च, तस्य
samasa.sense: the cosmic mountain at the centre of the world

morph.note: Perfect of √वृष्: reduplication व- and guṇa of ṛ (वर्ष्). The verb of raining takes the target in the accusative (देवीम्, शृङ्गम्) and what falls in the instrumental (शरवर्षेण, तोयवर्षेण).
The verb of the simile is not repeated: (वर्षति) ‘(rains on)’ is supplied from ववर्ष.

mantras.anvaya: सः असुरः समरे देवीं शरवर्षेण ववर्ष, यथा तोयदः मेरुगिरेः शृङ्गं तोयवर्षेण (वर्षति)।
mantras.anvaya_en: Main clause with ववर्ष; a simile introduced by यथा whose verb is understood from the main clause.
mantras.lit: He, the asura, rained on the Goddess in the battle with a rain of arrows, as a cloud (rains) on the peak of Mount Meru with a rain of water.
mantras.tr: In the battle the asura poured a storm of arrows on the Goddess, as a cloud pours its rain on the summit of Meru.

comm.t: The simile says what the arrows achieve: as much as rain does to Meru. The mountain is wetted, not moved.
A modern reading: the image places the attack and its target on different scales. What rains on the Goddess is weather; she is the mountain.

sandhi.note: After a short vowel an initial ch is doubled: a t is inserted and becomes c before ch. The Gita Press prints the two words together.
ā + e → ai. The same rule gives चैव (च + एव) in the second line.
Visarga after a vowel other than a/ā, before a voiced sound, appears as r.

morph.note: Absolutive of √छिद्: the d becomes t before -त्वा (छिद् + त्वा → छित्त्वा). It names the first of two acts by the same subject: she cut the arrows, then killed the horses.
Perfect of √हन्: reduplication ज- (h → j) and the root as -घान (h → gh after the reduplication, with vṛddhi in the 3rd singular).
Accusative singular of the tṛ-stem यन्तृ: यन्तारम्, like कर्तारम्. ‘The restrainer’ of the horses, i.e. the charioteer.

mantras.anvaya: ततः देवी लीलया एव तस्य शरोत्करान् छित्त्वा बाणैः तुरगान् वाजिनां यन्तारं च एव जघान।
mantras.anvaya_en: Absolutive clause (शरोत्करान् छित्त्वा) followed by the main verb जघान with two objects (तुरगान्, यन्तारम्).
mantras.lit: Then the Goddess, having cut his masses of arrows merely in play, struck down with arrows the horses and also the driver of the horses.
mantras.tr: The Goddess cut his arrows to pieces as if at play, and with her own arrows she killed his horses and their charioteer.

comm.t: The first answer is defensive, then she disables the chariot: horses and driver. लीलया एव — ‘just in play’ — repeats the phrase used of her at 2.50 (लीलयैव प्रचिच्छेद).
The ease of the Goddess (लीला) runs through the battle books: the same words recur at 8.31 and 10.13. The battle costs her nothing; the effort is all on the asuras’ side.

sandhi.note: -aḥ before the voiced dh becomes -o. Before s, धनुः keeps its visarga (धनुः सद्यो).

sandhi.type: consonant sandhi inside the word (prefix + participle)
sandhi.note: The d of उद् becomes c next to ś, and the ś after the stop becomes ch: उद् + श्रित → उच्छ्रित.

morph.note: Perfect of √छिद्: reduplication चि- (ch → c) with ch doubled after it (चि-च्छेद), and guṇa i → e.
Perfect of √व्यध्: the reduplicated syllable takes samprasāraṇa (व्य → वि), giving वि-व्याध with vṛddhi in the 3rd singular.
Three prefixes on one participle: अति ‘exceedingly’, सम् ‘wholly’, उद् ‘up’ with श्रित ‘resting’ — ‘raised very high’.
At the end of a bahuvrīhi धनुस् is replaced by the stem धन्वन्: acc. sg. -धन्वानम्, nom. sg. -धन्वा (as in 3.6).

mantras.anvaya: (देवी) सद्यः धनुः अतिसमुच्छ्रितं ध्वजं च चिच्छेद, छिन्नधन्वानं (तं) च एव आशुगैः गात्रेषु विव्याध।
mantras.anvaya_en: Subject (देवी) continued from 3.4; two coordinated verbs, चिच्छेद with two objects and विव्याध with one object, a locative of place and an instrument.
mantras.lit: And she at once cut (his) bow and the very lofty banner; and she also pierced in the limbs with swift-going (arrows) him whose bow was cut.
mantras.tr: At once she cut through his bow and his towering standard, and with swift arrows she pierced the disarmed asura all over his body.

comm.t: The chariot duel runs its course: horses and driver (3.4), bow and standard, then the warrior himself. The sequence follows the conventions of epic chariot combat.
The banner (ध्वज) is the warrior’s emblem; to cut it down is to announce his defeat before he falls.
